query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing part of the heavy Hf content with a small, controlled amount of aluminum in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower its overall density while preserving its high strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy having a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy’s composition by partially substituting Hf with Al (e.g. forming a composition such as Al_xHf_(1−x)MoTaTiZr with x in the range of about 0.2 to 0.4), thereby introducing a lightweight element into the matrix.
generation.conditions: The alloy is tested in its as‐cast state, with performance evaluated at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to around 1000 °C under similar loading conditions as the original alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Maintaining the single-phase (likely BCC) solid solution structure is critical; the Al addition is expected to induce a controlled lattice distortion similar to that of Hf while reducing the average atomic mass without triggering the formation of deleterious intermetallic or ordered phases.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s low atomic mass directly lowers the alloy density. At the same time, its incorporation into the solid solution can provide additional solid–solution strengthening via lattice distortion. When carefully balanced, this substitution does not significantly impair the dislocation mechanisms or phase stability responsible for high yield strength and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a density reduction (potentially a 10–15% decrease from 10.21 g/cm³, moving toward approximately 8.7–9.0 g/cm³) while retaining nearly the same yield strength and ductility at room temperature and ~1000 °C as that of the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: The original as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density ~10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high mechanical performance at RT and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The intervention is valid for as-cast alloys (without post-casting processing) and within the temperature range of RT to about 1000 °C. The level of Al substitution must be limited to avoid destabilizing the single-phase structure or inducing brittle intermetallic precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal fraction of Hf that can be replaced by Al without compromising the alloy’s mechanical properties is not yet determined. There is also uncertainty about the potential for formation of ordered phases if the Al content is too high and its effect on deformation mechanisms at high temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of as-cast alloys in which a controlled fraction of Hf is replaced by Al (for example, 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40% substitution levels in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy) while keeping the overall phase stability. Characterize the alloys using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and microstructural analysis to confirm that the solid-solution phase is retained. Then perform mechanical testing (tensile and/or compressive tests) at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
measurements: XRD and microstructural characterization (to verify phase retention and absence of brittle phases)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility) at room temperature and at ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any of the Al-substituted alloys either exhibit a significant reduction in yield strength or ductility at room temperature or at 1000 °C, or if the alloy develops undesirable secondary phases that compromise its mechanical integrity, then the hypothesis that partial substitution of Hf by Al reduces density without sacrificing mechanical properties would be falsified.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
